title: What space syntax is
text:
Space syntax describes where each street sits in the whole street network. It asks two questions about every street: how easy it is to reach from everywhere else, and how often it lies on the way between other places.
It looks at the shape of the network and nothing else. Shops and people are outside its view. I find that limit useful, because it lets me ask how much of Griffintown’s movement the layout alone can explain.

title: What space syntax is
text:
Where it comes from
Bill Hillier and Julienne Hanson started the method at University College London. Their book The Social Logic of Space (1984) argued that the arrangement of spaces carries social meaning and can be measured.








Year
Work
What it added




1993
Hillier, Penn, Hanson, Grajewski & Xu
“Natural movement”: the shape of the network is a main driver of how many people walk each street.


2004
Ratti
A critique: results depend on how the map is drawn, and early methods ignored metres.


2005
Hillier & Iida
Counting turns matched observed movement better than counting metres.


2007
Turner
Ordinary street centrelines can be analysed, so I can use the city’s own street file.



Full references are on the Resources page.






NoteHow settled is it?



The natural movement claim is influential and still debated. Its strength varies from place to place and depends on land use. In the 1993 paper itself, the correlation between integration and movement across ten parts of King’s Cross ranged from 0.25 to 0.80, and shops could outweigh the layout (Hillier et al. 1993, pp. 31, 46). Ratti (2004, p. 492) adds that the method leaves land use out. So in Situ I test the claim in Griffintown. I do not assume it.

title: What space syntax is
text:
Segments and depth
A segment is a piece of street between two junctions, the same unit as in S1 Streets. Depth is the distance between two segments. The made-up town below counts one step for each change of street, so it can be checked by hand. The real analysis counts angles: a right angle costs 1 and a 45° turn costs 0.5 (Turner 2007, p. 542). People seem to judge a route by how much it turns more than by its length (Hillier & Iida 2005).

title: What space syntax is
text:
Integration and choice
Integration measures how close a segment is, on average, to every other segment. A segment with high integration is easy to get to. Network science calls this closeness centrality (Sabidussi 1966).
Choice imagines the shortest route between every pair of segments and counts how many of those routes pass through each one. A segment with high choice is often passed through. Network science calls this betweenness centrality (Freeman 1977).

title: What space syntax is
text:
Radius
The analysis can be limited to a distance around each segment, called the radius. At 400 m it asks how central a street is within about five minutes’ walk. Radius n has no limit. In the literature, 400 to 800 m is the usual low radius and 4,000 to 8,000 m the usual high one (van Nes & Yamu 2021, p. 65).
My analysis (Sample 4) uses 200 to 800 m and radius n for pedestrians, and 1200 and 2000 m for vehicles. A street can be central at 400 m and peripheral at radius n, and that contrast often tells me more than any single value.

title: What space syntax is
text:
A made-up town
I invented this town so the numbers can be checked by hand. It has a main street (M1 to M5), cross streets to the north and south, a back street (B1, B2) and a cul-de-sac (C1, C2).



Depth from M1, then integration, then choice, on the same made-up town.



DepthIntegrationChoice


Starting from M1 at depth 0, every street one step away has depth 1, the next ones depth 2, and so on. C2, at the end of the cul-de-sac, is six steps away.


M3 has the highest integration (0.55), because it sits in the middle. C2 has the lowest (0.24), because every other street is far from it.


M4 has the highest choice (55), because routes from the west side to the east side and to the cul-de-sac must cross it. C1 has 15, since every route to C2 passes through it. A dead end like C2 scores 0.









TipWhat the toy shows



M3 is the best place to be, and M4 is the best place to pass through. The two measures differ, so I keep both.

title: What space syntax is
text:
The values in the results
The results also give normalised forms, NAIN for integration and NACH for choice, that can be compared between networks of different sizes (Hillier, Yang & Turner 2012, pp. 160, 165 and 191). NACH also evens out raw choice, where a few streets score very high and most score low. The paper gives two slightly different versions of NAIN, so I compare numbers only within one version (Reading closely).

The regulation numbers the turn bans P-110-6 to P-110-8, while the 2026 poster shows P-110-62 for “no left turn”. So S3 reads a sign’s written meaning and ignores its code number.


None of these says where a sign stands, before or after the junction. That does not say which corner. So placement has to be read from photos, one junction at a time (below).

title: Checking the sources
section: PlanX: how far is a radius?
text:
PlanX: how far is a radius?
PlanX is the QGIS tool that gives each street segment its space syntax values. Its manual (version 4.18, September 2026) says the radius is “metric radii in map units”. It does not say whether 800 m means 800 m along the streets or 800 m in a straight line. These give very different neighbourhoods, so I tested it.
For each segment, PlanX reports how many other segments it found within the radius. For twelve segments in Griffintown I counted again in two ways: segments I can walk to within the radius, along the streets, and segments whose middle lies inside a circle of that radius. At 800 m, PlanX’s counts came to 0.89 of the along-the-streets counts and 0.57 of the straight-line counts. At 400 m the figures were 0.92 and 0.53.
So the radius is measured along the streets (certain). PlanX’s counts sit a little under mine, most likely because it measures metres along the path with the fewest turns, which is a bit longer than the shortest path (likely). I could not reproduce the counts exactly, so that detail stays open.

title: Checking the sources
section: Mapillary: which way does a sign face?
text:
Mapillary: which way does a sign face?
Mapillary reads its street photos with a machine and places every sign it sees on a map, with a compass angle for each. If that angle is the way the sign faces, it can tell which street a sign controls. That is exactly what the sign sources above leave open.

Getting the signs
I asked Mapillary for every feature it has mapped around the S1 network, in squares of about 400 m because it refuses large ones, and kept the traffic signs unchanged, with the date. On 10 October that gave 1,455 signs, 838 of them regulatory, among them 235 stop detections and 88 no-entry signs.


Testing the direction on signs we already know
A stop sign faces the drivers it stops. S3 already knows, for every city stop post, which street those drivers arrive along. So the right answer is known in advance: the sign should face against the drivers’ travel. For each city stop post I took the nearest Mapillary stop sign within 15 m and compared.



Left: the idea. Right: the test. Pink bars are posts where Mapillary’s angle is within 45° of facing the drivers.


Of 139 city stop posts, 99 had a Mapillary stop sign within 15 m. For 69 of those, Mapillary’s angle was within 45° of facing the drivers, and only one pointed the way drivers travel. The median difference was 21°.
So the angle is the way the sign faces (likely). A second, smaller group sits near 90° off, and it has a simple cause (likely): at an all-way stop, four stop signs stand within a few metres, and the nearest Mapillary sign can be the one facing the cross street.
The main peak sits about 15° off zero, and I do not know why yet. Fifteen degrees never confuses two streets meeting at a junction, so it does not change how I use the angle. A machine reading is evidence to check, and every sign I use this way gets its photo looked at.

title: Checking the sources
text:
What changes in the systems
S3 reads each sign by its written meaning. Where a sign’s placement was in doubt, I settled it with Mapillary’s facing and then the photo (S3 checks with photos). S2 reads its radii as distance along the streets, and its vehicle values ignore one-way streets.

title: S4 Buildings
text:
S4 says what each building in the study area is: what it is used for, how tall it is, how many people live in it, and what is on its ground floor. It gathers this from six open files. Every answer keeps a note of where it came from. When no file knows the answer, the space stays empty with the reason written beside it.
Two more pages go further: how S4 is built and how I tested it.

title: S4 Buildings
text:
Why buildings matter here
S1 to S3 describe where people can move. They say nothing about why anyone would go somewhere. A street is busy at noon because of what lines it: a bank, a café, a gym, five hundred condos. S5 Rhythm will ask which buildings open when, and S6 will ask where people start and end their trips. S4 is the inventory they both read.
Most answers come from the city’s tax roll, the official list of every property and what it is. When the roll is silent, I fall back on OpenStreetMap, the open map anyone can edit. For the ground floor I use the city’s 2025 survey of street-level commercial spaces, together with the places listed in OpenStreetMap.
One answer is an assumption, and I label it as one: which street a walker reaches the building from. No open file says where the doors are, so I link each building to the nearest street people can walk on. It is the weakest value in S4.

title: S4 Buildings
text:
One building, step by step
District Griffin sur Peel is the long low block on Rue Peel between Ottawa and William, with towers on top. OpenStreetMap draws it as one outline and tags it as retail.
The tax roll has 496 properties on its lot. Almost all of them, 494, are condo dwellings. The other two are a shopping centre and a condo parking space. The roll speaks first, so S4 calls the building residential. The retail tag is kept on record and never used.
The 2025 survey finds ten premises on the ground floor, among them three banks and two restaurants. One space is vacant. Seven of these shops also appear in OpenStreetMap under the same name, so S4 counts each of them once. The nearest walkable street is Rue Ottawa, 6.5 m away.
This one building shows the main weakness of S4. Counted by property, the condos outvote the shops 494 to 1. On the street, though, it reads as a shopping strip. That is why I keep the ground floor separately: “used for” says what most of the building is, and “ground floor” says what a walker passes.

title: S4 Buildings
section: What I still need to check
text:
What I still need to check
S4 flags 61 cases for me to look at by hand. Most are buildings whose use no source gives. Some are ties, where two uses had the same number of properties. A few stand far from any walkable street, Hangar 1825 most of all. Ten times the city’s lot outline and its address point name different buildings. The largest was Griffix: its 197 flats had their address point inside MaryRobert next door, but their lot holds Griffix alone, so they now count in Griffix. And 415 properties stand at an address point far from any building.
That last one matters most. At 1485 rue des Bassins (B01), the tax roll lists 415 properties built in 2024: 290 dwellings and 125 condo parking spaces, all at one address point with no building on it. I first read this as a building OpenStreetMap had not drawn yet. The lot outlines changed my reading. The lot of 1485 holds Bass 4 and Le Vittorio, 130 m from the address point, and neither building has a single property placed in it. So the 290 dwellings most likely belong to those two towers, and the address point is the thing out of place (likely). Which tower holds how many, no file says. Until a door number or a site visit settles it, I leave them unplaced and counted, and I split nothing by guess.

title: S4 Buildings
text:
A note on licences
The Concordia NGCI building file has heights and a use for every building in Montréal, but it carries no licence. S4 does not use it, and I publish nothing made from it until a licence is granted.

title: S3 tests
text:
Stress tests
Each stress test changes one thing on purpose and counts how many rules move. The first, X1, simply runs S3 twice on the same input. The results are identical.
X2 moves every sign post at random, by up to 1, 2, 4 and 8 m. Up to 2 m almost nothing changes. At 4 m ten streets change their stop, and at 8 m, 28 do. So the city’s sign positions would have to be off by more than 2 m before the stop rules start to shift. I do not know yet how accurate they are, and that is worth checking on the ground at a few corners.



X2: as every post is moved further, more rules change. Up to 2 m almost nothing moves. Click to enlarge.


X3 and X4 change how far before the junction, and how far to the right, a sign may stand. Both sit on a plateau: a little more or less than my 35 m and 20 m changes nothing, so the result does not hang on my exact choice. Only the tightest values lose signs. Most of the signs without a street stand at exits or beyond the edge.
X5 places turn signs by position alone, as my first version did. That leaves 25 streets with no turn at all, against none with the meaning test and the photo decisions. That is why the meaning test exists.
X6 changes how close a light must be to its junction. From 25 to 40 m the same 31 junctions get lights. At 5 m eight are lost: those lights stand 5 to 10 m from their junctions, mostly on Robert-Bourassa and on edge streets, where the city places the light on a wide corner. At 80 m, lights start landing on the wrong junctions.
X7 changes how far a same-name line may lie when a street is missing from the speed file. It is the one setting with no plateau below it. Under 5 m, two Wellington pieces open to cars lose their limit. From 5 m on, all three redrawn pieces are covered. The 5 m was chosen for those three segments, and how S3 is built says so. Autoroute 10 and its ramps are never in the file, at any distance.

I start from a place S3 could not settle, and gather the signs Mapillary detected within 30 m of the junction (getting the signs).
For each sign there are two readings of where it faces. One is Mapillary’s own angle, which I tested on stop signs. The other comes from the photo itself: a sign whose face I can read is turned towards the camera. Each reading then points to the street whose drivers the sign faces.
The tool cuts the sign out of each panorama and puts every photo of one junction on one sheet, next to what the machine read. I look at the sheet and write down one decision per finding, with how sure I am and the evidence. The city’s file is never edited. At the next build S3 reads my decisions before its own matching.
I call a decision likely when the two readings point to the same street and the photo shows a sign that fits. I leave it open when the readings disagree or the photo does not show which way the sign faces. A sign newer than every photo stays open too.

The green “straight only” on the west elm corner was seen in May 2022 and December 2023, and both readings point to Wellington arriving from the west. title: S2 tests
text:
Stress tests
The checks ask whether the result is right. The stress tests ask how easily it could go wrong. Each one changes one thing on purpose and measures what moves.
Running twice on the same input gives identical results, and changing the matching distance anywhere from 5 cm to 10 m changes nothing. Placing test points every 25 cm or every 5 m moves a value by about 0.01 at most.
Shaking every S1 point by up to 0.3 m changes one segment, a 15 m connector at Brennan, which then takes part of its value from the next connector. Shaken by up to 0.8 m, six segments change status, mostly paths and connectors along the canal, and no value moves by more than 0.08.
The real test is the same-kind rule. With the rule turned off and nothing shaken, no segment takes values from another line. Shaken by 0.8 m, 142 segments do. The worst is the short Smith link, which then takes values from the streets at both its ends and moves by 0.24.



As the S1 points are shaken further, segments without the same-kind rule start taking values from crossing streets. With the rule, almost nothing moves.


What I take from this: the match is exact today because S1 and the walking network share coordinates, which is why the matching distance has no effect. The same-kind rule is what would keep S2 honest if the geometry drifted, for example after someone edits S1 in QGIS.
The rule test also found a real fault upstream. Before a fix, Rue Smith picked up 21 m from a connector, which meant a connector lay on top of the street. It was the C06 link, which joined Smith to its own other end. I fixed the rule in S1 (C06), and after the new PlanX run no such segment remains.

title: How S2 is built
text:
The problem
S1 and the walking network were built from the same city lines, and each one cut those lines in its own places. S1 cut a street where a park path joins it. The walking network cut streets wherever a bike path joins them, all over the island. So an S1 segment and an analysed line are often the same street with different ends.
Matching by id alone would hide that. Rue des Seigneurs, for example, is one S1 segment lying over two analysed pieces with different values. Matching by shape finds both.

title: How S2 is built
text:
The matching rule



A made-up segment and the analysed lines under it.


I cut each S1 segment into slices about a metre long and place a test point in the middle of each. Each point looks for the closest analysed line within 1 m, but only among lines of the same kind. A city street looks only at pieces of the same street in the city’s records, and a path or connector looks only at its own kind.
Then I count the metres each analysed line shares with the segment. The cover is the share of the segment’s length that found a line. The value is the mean of those lines, each counting by the metres it shares, so with one line it is that line’s value exactly. The cover decides the status. Below 50 % the segment gets no value, and the reason is written down.
The same-kind rule matters near junctions. A test point near the end of a street also lies within 1 m of the crossing street. Without the rule, the street could take some of its neighbour’s values. The stress tests measure that risk.

title: How S2 is built
text:
Vehicle values
The driving network keeps the city’s lines uncut, so the city’s own street id is enough. Every S1 piece of a street gets that street’s vehicle value.
Before looking the street up, S2 checks whether cars may use it, by the same rule S1 uses. A street closed to cars is marked as not a road, with a written reason, and so is every added path or connector. That makes 37 segments, each meant to be empty. A street cars may use that is missing from the analysis would be marked missing. Today there are none.

title: S1 Streets
text:
S1 turns the city’s street lines into a network of segments and junctions, and records who may use each segment. Every later system walks or drives on this network, so it has to be right first.
How S1 is built sets out the rules I assumed. Two pages then test it: the tests check the network against itself, and Checks and decisions check it against the real street, with photos.

title: S1 Streets
text:
Words



A made-up street that shows every word S1 uses.


A segment is a piece of street between two junctions, and a junction is where segment ends meet. Griffintown stays part of the city, so S1 also keeps the streets just outside the boundary that touch the study area. I call them the edge. A gate is where the study area meets the edge, and an exit is the far end of an edge street, where the city carries on. A dead end is a junction with only one segment that is neither a gate nor an exit. A one-way arrow shows the only direction cars may use; pedestrians may always walk both ways.
S1 starts from the city’s street lines, which already carry the space syntax results, and the outline of the study area. My decisions from the checks are applied on top, each with its evidence. Every segment keeps the city’s own id, so any value can be traced back to its source.

What changed in October
The October rebuild came from decisions about the boundary and about a few street ends. Every segment and junction that existed before kept its number. Pieces from later decisions are numbered last, so confirming or rejecting one never renumbers anything else.
The boundary first. The city codes Boulevard Robert-Bourassa as a pair of one-way roads about 60 m apart, and the boundary ran between them, so the boulevard carried traffic one way only. S1 now takes in both (C19), and keeps the edge around the whole area.
Then the street ends. A footway now runs from the end of Brennan through the block to de la Commune (C04, C12), and the end of Ann joins it (C05). These links are assumed, and drawn in pink until a photo or a visit confirms them. From the end of Smith, a 41 m link crosses the plaza of Place des Aiguilleurs (C06). title: S1 Streets
section: Try it: from here to there
text:
Try it: from here to there
In the Lab, choose S1, then “from here to there”, and click a start junction and an end junction. Everything it shows comes from the network alone:







Measure
What it tells you




Shortest route
the shortest way along the streets, on foot or by car; every other route is compared with it


Directness
the route’s length divided by the straight line between the two points. A grid gives about 1.3; a barrier such as the canal pushes it higher


Variety
in pink, every street you could pass through on a trip at most 0, 5, 10, 25 or 50 % longer than the shortest. A wide band means many ways to go; a thin one means the layout funnels everyone onto one street


Cost of one-way streets
by car, how much longer the drive is than the walk between the same two junctions



A good first example is William at Young to further along William. It is 306 m on foot and 966 m by car, because William is one-way and the car has to go round the block.
Two trips from Rue des Bassins show the difference between the grid and the canal. From Bassins at Rioux to Notre-Dame at Robert-Bourassa, a 10 % detour opens up 82 other segments: walkers have many ways. From Bassins at Allée des Barges to Wellington, the walk is 1.7 times the straight line, because the canal has few crossings.
These measures say nothing about how anyone actually chooses a route. People do not all take the shortest way, and the turn bans and stops of S3 are not counted here. Routes also stay inside the study area, so by car many trips cannot be made without the city outside, and the Lab says so when that happens. Choice belongs to S6 Walkers and S7 Drivers; these measures are the yardstick their routes will be compared with. Lab notes shows how the measures are tested.

Notes
A road map is a poor walking map. The city’s file left out the canal path and the new park paths, and 10 of the 12 dead ends turned out to be places where walkers continue.
The boundary is a drawing decision. A line through the middle of a boulevard cut its traffic in half.
Street View can be old. Some of my evidence dates from 2007 to 2016, so every decision keeps its date.
One step of the reach is one junction. Distances in metres are in the route tool. Time comes later, when S6 and S7 give walkers and cars a speed.

title: How S1 is built
text:
The edge
Griffintown is part of Montréal, and people and cars come and go. So S1 keeps every city street just outside the boundary that touches the study area, and calls it the edge. A gate is a junction where the study area meets the edge. An exit is the far end of an edge street: the tests, and later the agents, treat the rest of the city as reachable from there.
The edge follows the same rules as the inside, for walkers and for the direction of cars. S3 reads its signs too, so a junction on the boundary sees every street that meets it. Later systems decide what to do with it: S4 puts no buildings there, and S8 measures inside the boundary only.
Pieces from decisions taken after the October rebuild are numbered after everything else, the edge included. Confirming or rejecting one of them then never changes another id.

title: How S1 is built
text:
Two ideas behind it

Inside or outside?How far can I get?


To decide whether a point lies inside the study area, imagine a line going right from it and count how many times it crosses the outline. An odd count means inside. This is called ray casting. S1 applies it to the halfway point of each segment.


Start at one junction and take every allowed move, then every move from each place you reached, and so on. This is called breadth-first search, and each round is one step. The reach view in the Lab plays it round by round.

title: Reading closely
text: Many sentences on this site lean on a book or a paper. In October I went back to each of those texts with the page open, to see whether my sentence still said what the author said. Most did. A few had drifted, usually by a small step, and the drift was always in the same direction: towards what my model needed the reading to say. Those few cases taught me more than the rest, so this page is about them.

title: Reading closely
text:
Where my sentences had drifted
I had written that people “tend to keep going roughly straight”, citing Hillier and Iida. Their claim is narrower. People judge routes by how much they turn (Hillier & Iida 2005, p. 476), which is a statement about how routes are compared, and says little about what a walker does at each corner. The difference will matter when S6 gives walkers a way to choose their routes.
I had also written that 2000 m is a common radius for driving. Hillier, Yang and Turner call radius 2000 “safe to use” for cities in general (2012, p. 165). They say nothing about cars. Using it for driving is my choice, and the S2 page now says so.
A third sentence claimed that walkers who always take the route with the least turning would reproduce the choice values by construction. That holds only if trips are spread evenly over every pair of places (Turner 2007, p. 544). Real trips are not, since people go to work and to shops far more often than to a random corner. I added the condition.
The last case is about my own reading. The definition of a spatial culture I use comes from Hillier (1989), but I know it only through Griffiths and von Lünen’s quotation of it (2016, p. xxiii). I have kept it, and I say plainly that it is second-hand.

title: Reading closely
section: What held, and what it leaves open
text:
What held, and what it leaves open
The claim the whole method rests on did hold. Hillier and his colleagues found that the layout of the street network is “the main generator of patterns of movement” (1993, p. 29). The same paper also shows how much that depends on place: across ten parts of King’s Cross, the correlation between layout and counted movement ranges from 0.25 to 0.80 (p. 46), and shops can multiply movement beyond what the layout predicts (p. 31). Ratti (2004) adds that the results shift with how the map is drawn. I read these together as a reason to use space syntax as a measuring stick, never as the engine of the simulation (why).

title: Reading closely
section: Checking the software against the papers
text:
Checking the software against the papers
PlanX, the plugin I use for the analysis, follows the published measures, with two details worth knowing.

Does PlanX count a journey once, or once each way?
PlanX’s manual leaves this open, and its own output answers it. Take a street segment that leads into a dead end and meets only two other lines at its far end. Every journey from the dead end passes through it, and no other journey does, so its choice value is simply the number of those journeys. In 103 such cases, PlanX’s value is the number counted once per pair of places, never the doubled one. So PlanX counts each pair once, as Turner defines choice (2007, p. 544). Another tool that counted both ways would give somewhat higher normalised choice values (likely), which matters before comparing Griffintown with a published study.


Which NAIN?
For normalised choice (NACH), PlanX reproduces the published formula exactly. For normalised integration (NAIN), the paper gives one form in its text and another in its appendix, and PlanX uses a third.



Form
Where it appears
Matches PlanX

The three forms rank the streets almost identically, so the maps do not change. The numbers themselves do differ, so a NAIN from this site should only be compared with one computed the same way.
As a last check, Hillier, Yang and Turner (2012, p. 162) report that real cities have a mean NACH between about 0.7 and 1.2. Montréal on my walking network has 0.80, which suggests the network was built and analysed in an ordinary way.

title: Reading closely
text:
Still to read
Decoding the City by Offenhuber and Ratti (2014) will matter once the project turns to images and video of the street. The Depthmap handbook and manual will matter when I compare PlanX with Depthmap. Where this site cites Lefebvre’s Rhythmanalysis and the archival readings, the pages are given beside each quotation.
Close reading has a limit of its own. It tells me whether a sentence matches its source, and nothing about whether the source is right. Several of these readings are still debated, and I try to say so where I use them.

title: Limits of the desk
text:
So far I have built Situ from open data, and I have looked at Griffintown mostly through other people’s cameras. I have not yet walked the area with a notebook to check each place myself. That shapes what every system can claim. This page sets out those limits in one place, so a reader can weigh each result against the way it was made.
Two words help. By open data I mean files that public bodies or volunteers publish for anyone to use, such as the city’s tax roll or OpenStreetMap. By desk research I mean everything I can do from a screen: working with those files, and looking at photos and videos that someone else took.

title: Limits of the desk
section: A file is made for its own purpose
text:
A file is made for its own purpose
No file describes a city in general. Each one was made by an institution to do a job, and its categories serve that job. Scholars of data make the same point: data are gathered and shaped for a purpose before anyone analyses them (Gitelman 2013; Kitchin 2014). When I borrow a file for a different question, its categories come with it.
The city’s street file is a road file. It left out the canal path and the new park paths, and 10 of the first 12 dead ends in S1 turned out to be places where walkers carry on. The tax roll is a file for taxing property. It counts a condo parking space as a property, as it counts a home, and it gives a tower’s storeys only for some kinds of property. The sign inventory serves the crews who maintain signs. It says where a sign stands and what it says, and never which way it faces.

title: Limits of the desk
section: Four ways the files fall short
text:
Four ways the files fall short
Purpose is one limit. I meet three more again and again.
The first is time. Every file has its own date, and Griffintown changes faster than most of them. Some of my Street View evidence dates from 2007 to 2016. The city’s sign post at one corner under the Wellington viaduct is from October 2025, while every photo of it is older (P03). The city’s 3D model of 2020 covers Ville-Marie and stops at the borough line, so Griffintown, in Le Sud-Ouest, has only the model of 2016, older than many of its towers. When two files disagree, the cause is often a gap in time.
The second is coverage: what a file leaves out. The speed file has no limits for Autoroute 10 and its ramps. The traffic light file says where the lights are and nothing about their timing. No open file says where the doors of buildings are. OpenStreetMap is drawn by volunteers, so a building appears only once someone draws it.
The third is position. A point in a file stands in for a thing on the street, and the two are rarely in the same spot. An address point often stands at the curb and a shop’s point on its façade. At 1485 rue des Bassins, 290 dwellings share one address point that stands 130 m from the two towers on their lot (checkpoint B01). Even my own arithmetic can move things: an early version of S4 placed some building centres tens of metres off, because of the way it handled large map coordinates.

title: Limits of the desk
text:
Seeing from the desk
Photos and videos let me look at the street without being there, and they settled real questions. Mapillary photos from 2016 and 2024 showed that walkers cross Place des Aiguilleurs at the end of Rue Smith (C06). Photos settled most of the no-entry disagreements in S3. A walking video filmed on 11 July 2026 shows the signs at the entrance of Allée des Vraquiers: no entry except for emergency vehicles, a pedestrian zone, no bicycles.
Still, a camera goes where its owner walks, and it records one moment. Neither of the two recent walking videos reaches the end of Rue Brennan, so the footway I assumed there (C04) is still unconfirmed. A sign seen edge-on shows that it exists and hides which street it faces. A photo older than the sign it shows can mislead.

title: Limits of the desk
text:
People are missing
The deepest limit is about people. Open data records a city’s infrastructure, its streets and its properties. Apart from the city’s movement counts at a few intersections (Movement counts), it says almost nothing about how people use the streets: where they linger, or when a corner fills. Situ wants to mediate and archive spatial culture and urban rhythm, and those live in what people do. From the desk I can describe the stage. I cannot yet describe the play.

title: Limits of the desk
text:
How Situ carries the gaps
I try to keep each gap visible. A value no source gives stays empty, with the reason written beside it, and is never filled with a zero or a guess. Every assumption is labelled as one, on the page and in the Lab. Every place the desk could not settle becomes a checkpoint with a question, and the Lab explains why each kind matters.
Most of the remaining checkpoints can only be closed on site. The next step is a walk through Griffintown with these questions in hand, photographing and dating each answer. Later, observation of people in place will feed S5 Rhythm, the first system about time and use.

title: Lab notes
text:
The Lab is one map with a tab for each system. Each system page keeps its own blueprint and maps. The Lab is where I can try a system, see the places it still leaves open, and click anything on the map to read what every system knows about it.
The Lab replays results. It never recomputes them. Every street colour and every slider position shows a result a system already wrote down. One tool is an exception, and I kept it small. Storing every route between every pair of junctions would make a file of many megabytes. So I store only the shortest distances and the last step of each shortest route, and the Lab applies two short rules to them: follow the route back, and test each street against the detour allowed. Those two rules are written twice, once beside the systems and once in the browser, and a test runs both on 45,600 cases to check they give the same streets.

title: Movement counts and light timing
section: Why the lights need an estimate
text:
Why the lights need an estimate
S3 knows where the 31 lights in S1 are. It does not know how long they stay green, because the city does not publish its timing plans. So the timing has to be estimated, and the estimate is mine.

title: Movement counts and light timing
text:
Webster’s method
Webster’s method (Webster 1958) is the classic way to set a fixed light cycle from counted traffic. It asks how full each approach is, and which cycle length keeps the delay smallest. I apply it to the busiest counted hour.
How full an approach is means the cars arriving per hour (a bus or truck counts as two) divided by what its lanes can pass while green, about 1,800 cars an hour per lane. The lanes come from OpenStreetMap. Each phase of the light takes its fullest approach, and the phases add up to a total load. Webster’s formula turns that total, and the time lost each time the green changes (4 s per phase here), into a cycle length. Each phase then gets green in proportion to its load.
I add one check Webster does not make. A pedestrian crossing during a phase needs at least 7 s to start, plus the time to cross at a walking speed of 1.2 m/s. Where the green is shorter, I lengthen it.
The two phases run along Montréal’s north-south, then its east-west. “North” here means the street grid’s north, about 305° on the compass, as in the city’s counts. The counts confirm it: at J040 almost nothing arrives from the north, where Ottawa is the one street no car may arrive along.



The estimated cycles, second by second. Grey: amber and all-red, the time lost when the green changes.

title: Movement counts and light timing
text:
What it shows
At J040 (Guy, Ottawa and William), at 16h on 18 December 2024, the total load was 0.29 and Webster’s cycle came to 24 s. At J051 (de la Montagne and Notre-Dame) the load was 0.38 and the cycle 27 s.
The traffic is far from filling these lights. Cycles of 24 and 27 s are much shorter than any city would use, so the cycle I use is my lower limit of 60 s. The green is then set by pedestrians and by the split of loads: 26 s each way at J040, and 38 s north-south against 14 s east-west at J051. That is a finding about Griffintown’s streets, and also a warning: at these volumes, the timing is more a design choice than a consequence of traffic.
J181, on Robert-Bourassa, is skipped. Three of its four approaches lie beyond the network, and Webster needs them all.

title: Movement counts and light timing
text:
The other 29 lights
I weighed four options. One plan for all lights would be simple, but a main street and a side street would get the same green. Borrowing the split of a counted light on the same streets would use real counts, but only two lights were counted. Timing the lights from space syntax was ruled out: S8 compares movement with space syntax, and lights timed from it would make S8 measure its own input. I chose to share the green by road class, which uses the city’s own street hierarchy, already in S1.

Why road class
The city’s 2007 review of its arterial network (PDF) gives each class a daily traffic range: main arteries carry over 30,000 vehicles, collectors 1,000 to 15,000. Managing the flow is “prépondérante” on main arteries and “peu” on collectors (Ville de Montréal 2007). The United States standard says the same: “In general, the higher the traffic volume is, the higher the functional classification will be” (FHWA 2023, p. 26, PDF). And Webster (1958) shares the green in proportion to how full each approach is, so a busier street should get more of it.


Testing it on our counts
At every counted junction where the two streets differ in class, the higher class carried more traffic over the counted day:

Five out of five, though four are on Wellington, so the sample is small. And road class does not match Webster at the two counted lights. At J040 it would give 21 and 31 s where Webster gives 26 and 26, because at the busiest hour each lane is about as full on both streets. At J051 it would give 26 and 26 s where Webster gives 38 and 14, because the classes are equal but de la Montagne is busier. So the class tells which street gets more green over a day. It cannot tell how much at a given hour. That is why the counted lights keep Webster, and why the share by class is a cautious 60 %.


The rule
Each street arriving at a light belongs to one of the two axes, and each axis takes the highest class among its streets: main arterial (with highway) above secondary arterial, above collector, above local. If both axes have the same class, the two phases share the 52 s of usable green equally. If not, the higher class gets 60 % and the lower 40 %. No phase is shorter than its pedestrians need, and where they need more, the cycle grows. Where cars arrive on one axis only, the other phase is for pedestrians.
Of the 31 lights, 2 follow Webster from counts, 17 have one street of higher class, 7 have equal classes, and 5 have cars on one axis only, mostly at the edge where the cross street lies beyond the network. In S7 these become the light plans, and the 60 % share and the 60 s cycle will be sliders in the Lab.

text:
Assumptions
Every number here is a choice, and two are mine alone. The 60 s lower limit on the cycle (with 120 s as the upper) is my guess for a city centre, and it sets every cycle here. The 60 % share is my own choice: the counts show which street is busier, and say nothing of the amount. The other values (lane capacity, time lost per phase, walking speed and walk interval) follow Webster or common practice; real amber and all-red times are not published, and Montréal does not publish its own walking speed. The lane counts from OpenStreetMap cover 866 of 870 car ways, and I checked them at three junctions only.
The counts themselves are a few days each, in winter or spring. They show those days, not a typical year.

title: About Situ
text:
Situ is the prototype for my PhD research-creation project. It asks whether the spatial culture and urban rhythm of Griffintown, Montréal, can be mediated and archived through a game-like 3D experience. I look at two eras: today, and the 1920s to 1940s. I work from the city’s open data and from observation, and I read both through urban theory. Game design carries the result to a player.
Nothing in Situ archives anything yet. So far there is a foundation: the street network with its rules, and the measures I will test it against.

title: About Situ
text:
The idea

Spatial culture
Hillier described a spatial culture as “a distinctive way of ordering space” (Hillier 1989, quoted in Griffiths & von Lünen 2016, p. xxiii). Griffiths and von Lünen see the field as the link between how a built place works and what it comes to mean to the people who live in it (2016, p. xxi). Adams (2024, introduction) wants spatial culture to be “qualified and documented”, which is close to what an archive needs.


Rhythm
A street layout has no time in it, and space syntax tends to strip social practice of its time (Griffiths & von Lünen 2016, p. xxiii). Lefebvre finds rhythm wherever energy is spent in a particular place and time (2004, p. 15). His own example is a Paris junction seen from his window: on red the pedestrians cross, on green the cars rush (p. 28). The light cycles in S3 model that beat. He also holds that where there is rhythm there is measure (p. 8), so counts and timings belong in Situ. I add time on purpose: when places are open and when streets are busy.


Archiving
An archive keeps two things: the evidence records give of how their maker worked, and the information they hold about people and places (Schellenberg 1956, pp. 139 to 140). Situ keeps both. The city data says what Griffintown is. My decision files and tests record how I turned it into a model, the layer the London Charter calls paradata (2009, principle 4.6). The Seville principles ask that a reconstruction show what is real and what is not (López-Menchero & Grande, principle 4), and that others can test it (principle 7). So every decision in my files carries a status, such as confirmed, assumed, likely or open.
Rhythm is the hard part. Taylor separates the archive of lasting things from the repertoire of embodied practice, like walking to work or lingering at a corner, which needs people to be present (2003, pp. 19 to 20). Situ cannot store a rhythm the way it stores a street. It can keep traces such as counts and timings, and offer a place where the rhythm can be performed again: the game. The Seville principles warn against showing “lifeless cities” (principle 5.3).


What Situ has and what it lacks
Lefebvre describes three moments of social space (1991, pp. 38 to 40). I use them as a checklist. He warns that they lose their force when treated as an abstract model (p. 40), so each row stays open to revision.

NoteFour readings I make, and how I defend them





These are my own interpretations of the sources. For each one I give my reason, the strongest objection I know, my answer, and what would show me wrong.

1. Lefebvre’s triad as a checklist

Reason. Each kind of source in Situ lines up with one of Lefebvre’s moments of social space (1991, pp. 38 to 40).
Objection. He warns that the triad loses its force as an abstract model (p. 40), and laying it over software comes close to that.
Answer. I use it only to see what is missing, and the lived row is empty. The rows also leak: the counts are observation, yet the city decided where to count.
Wrong if the rows cannot be kept apart at all. Then the table should show the crossings.



2. “That difference is what the archive should keep”

Reason. Where space syntax and observed movement disagree, something besides the layout is at work, such as a shop or a rule. Griffiths and von Lünen ask research to spell out that kind of gap (2016, p. xxi), and the 1993 natural movement paper itself shows shops multiplying the effect of the layout (Hillier et al. 1993, p. 31).
Objection. A difference may only be error, such as a wrong network or too few counts.
Answer. So every system is tested, and a difference counts only after those checks.
Wrong if the differences vanish once errors are fixed, or follow no pattern.



3. Schellenberg’s two values

Reason. Schellenberg separates evidence of how a record’s maker worked from information about people and places (1956, pp. 139 to 140, 148). My decision files are the first kind and the city data is the second. The London Charter calls the first layer paradata (2009, principle 4.6).
Objection. He wrote about government records in 1956, and a research model is no government agency.
Answer. I borrow only his distinction, which he says he defines “quite arbitrarily” (p. 139). The London Charter already carries it into visualisation.
Wrong if the two layers cannot be kept apart. That is why my corrections live in their own file and the city’s files stay untouched.



4. Rhythm as repertoire, and the game as a place to perform it again

Reason. Taylor’s repertoire is embodied practice that needs people to be present (2003, pp. 19 to 20), and Lefebvre’s rhythm needs bodies spending energy (2004, p. 15). Play is embodied action too.
Objection. A player alone in a simulation receives no memory from Griffintown’s people, and the game itself is code and data, an archive object. Lefebvre adds that the rhythmanalyst is closer to the poet than to “the statistician, who counts things” (2004, p. 23).
Answer. I accept most of this. The game keeps traces and sets up a new performance. It does not hold the original repertoire, which is why interviews and focus groups are in the plan.
Wrong if players’ movement bears no relation to the recorded rhythms. Then the game performs nothing of Griffintown.







Space syntax as one measuring stick
Space syntax describes the layout. I use it to measure, and the simulated walkers never read it. At the end, S8 compares where they went with what space syntax predicts and with the city’s counts. Where they agree, the layout may explain the movement. Where they differ, something else is at work, and that difference is what the archive should keep. Why I use it

What changed

Taken outAdded


Highways come out, because nobody walks on them, and so do streets that exist only as plans.
Bike lanes painted on a street stay out, and so do paths lying on top of a street, since the street is already there and would be drawn twice. Added pieces that join nothing are dropped too, because a piece on its own would get meaningless values.


I added the off-street bike and multi-use paths from the city’s bike network, because people walk on them. Some of these paths are filed under a highway, mostly the separated paths on bridges. Removing the highway would have removed them as well, so I put them back. I also added the two Griffintown park paths I checked on photos in S1 (decision C18).

NoteEach step in plain words





A path counts as a duplicate when most of its length runs within 10 m of a street. It stays out.
Joining follows the same rules as S1. A path end joins the nearest junction or street, and a street dead end may join the middle of a path. Across most of the island the gap may be at most 15 m. In Griffintown, and at places I have checked on a photo, it may be 25 m, because there I have looked and can trust a longer gap. Nobody has looked at the rest of the island, so the rule stays strict there. When a path crosses a street with no junction, I leave it unjoined, since the crossing could be a bridge or a tunnel.
Where a connector lands in the middle of a street, the street is split at that point so the path has a junction to meet. Its total length stays the same.
Finally, every line is grouped with the lines it touches. Added pieces outside the main group are dropped. City streets are never dropped; if one is cut off, a check reports it.

title: The walking network
text:
Risks
A connector could join two things that are separate in reality. To guard against that, the gaps allowed are short and every connector is listed. Crossings are never joined automatically. The opposite can happen too: a real link stays unjoined. The 73 crossings are listed, and I can add checked places one by one.
Bike paths stand in for footpaths, and a few may be unpleasant or closed to walking, so I took only separated paths and multi-use trails. The city maps park footpaths less well than bike paths, and I checked only Griffintown on photos, so values far from it are less certain.
Near Griffintown the risk is low. Within 800 m there is one unjoined crossing, and within 2 km there are four.

title: The walking network
text:
The analysis
On 10 October I ran PlanX on this network with the Sample 4 pedestrian settings: angular segment analysis, at radii of 200, 400 and 800 m and the whole network. Every line kept its number and its shape, so S2 can trace each value back to one line.
My first run that day included a faulty first version of the Smith link (C06), which joined Smith to itself (how it was found). I rebuilt the network with the real link and ran PlanX again that evening with the same settings. A line-by-line check shows the result matches the network.

title: The walking network
text:
The driving network
The network for the vehicle analysis follows the same rules. It starts from every city line and leaves out the lines cars may not use under the S1 road classes, plus one small group of streets no car can reach from the rest. The lines it keeps stay exactly as the city drew them. Highways stay in, because cars use them. One-way streets keep their direction in the data, but segment analysis reads every line as two-way.
I ran PlanX on it on 10 October, at radii of 1200 and 2000 m. Before October the vehicle values came from Sample 4, which included pedestrian ways, so 31 segments closed to cars carried vehicle values. Now none do.

text:
S2 takes the space syntax values and attaches them to every S1 segment, and it records which analysed line each value came from. Later systems never read these values. Only S8 Observer uses them, at the very end, as a measuring stick (why).
Two kinds of value matter most here. Choice is roughly how often a street lies on the way between other places. Integration is roughly how easy a street is to reach. Both are measured within a radius, from 200 m up to the whole island.

title: S2 Scores
text:
How a value is found
The values come from PlanX’s analysis of the walking network and the driving network, where each analysed line carries its own values. For every S1 segment I look for the analysed lines lying under it, within 1 m. If two pieces of the same street lie under one segment, its value is their mean, weighted by length. A segment that finds too little gets no value at all, never a zero, and a written reason.

title: S2 Scores
text:
Result

257 of 264 segments with walking values · 227 with vehicle values

Almost every segment found its street exactly: 251 match one analysed line. Six are split across two pieces of the same street, such as Rue des Seigneurs and Rue Wellington, because the walking network cut those lines where a path joins and S1 did not.
Seven segments have no walking value. All seven are Autoroute 10 and its ramps. Highways were left out of the walking network, so their values stay empty.
Thirty-seven segments have no vehicle value, and none should. They are walking paths and connectors, or city streets cars may not use, like the Allées or the pedestrian ends of Murray and Smith. No segment closed to cars carries a vehicle value. Before October there were 31, because the older Sample 4 vehicle analysis included pedestrian ways.



How each segment was matched. Grey: matched cleanly. Pink: the exceptions, numbered and explained in the key.

title: S2 Scores
text:
What changed in October
On 10 October I reran both analyses on the rebuilt networks and compared each segment inside Griffintown with its old value. Most streets kept their place in the order: the rank agreement (Spearman’s correlation, where 1.00 means no street moved) was 0.99 or 1.00 for every measure I compared.
Two changes are real, and both come from my own decisions. Rue Brennan and Rue Ann gained walking choice: the east end of Brennan went from 0.00 to 0.90, and Ann from 0.37 to 0.93. Both now lead somewhere, because I assumed they connect to the paths beyond them. That is an assumption. If a photo shows those streets really stop, I will reject those decisions and the values will fall back.
Murray and Smith lost vehicle choice. The driving network leaves out their pedestrian ends, by the same road rule S1 uses. In the analysis cars can no longer pass through there, so the street before carries less through-traffic.

title: How S3 is built
text:
The problem
The city’s sign file gives each post a position and a list of panels. It does not say which street a sign faces. A stop sign at a corner stands close to two or three streets at once, and only one of them has to stop. So for each sign, S3 has to work out which street it was put there for.

title: How S3 is built
text:
Approaches
A sign speaks to the drivers coming from one direction. So S3 first lists every approach: each end of each street segment, seen as a car drives towards the junction. For each approach it notes four things: the direction a car is heading as it arrives, whether the one-way rules let a car arrive or leave along it, how long the segment is, and whether the junction is an exit, where the edge street meets the rest of the city.
The end of a one-way street pointing away from the junction gets no rules, since no car arrives that way.

title: How S3 is built
section: How a stop sign finds its street
text:
How a stop sign finds its street



A made-up junction. Left: where a stop sign must stand to belong to a street. Right: how a turn gets its name. Click to enlarge. To try it on real junctions, open the Lab.


In Québec a stop sign usually stands on the right of the street, just before the junction. S3 relies on that.
For each post, S3 looks at the approaches nearby and measures two distances: how far before the junction the post stands, and how far to the right of the street’s centre line. A post fits an approach when it stands up to 35 m before the junction and between 1 and 20 m to the right. It must also stand on that segment: a post further back belongs to the previous junction. This matters on very short pieces, like the 20 m stretches where Wellington splits in two.
If several approaches fit, the one closest to the usual spot wins (about 7 m to the right, near the junction), and S3 marks the link as less sure. On a one-way street signs often stand on both sides, so a post on the left is accepted too. If nothing fits, the sign gets no street and goes on the list to check.

title: How S3 is built
section: How a turn sign finds its street
text:
How a turn sign finds its street
Turn signs are harder. They often stand across the junction or on a median, so where a turn sign stands is a weak clue. S3 adds a second clue: what the sign would mean on each street nearby.
Back at J027, both signs say “left turn only”, and two streets are close enough to own them. On Rue Chatham a car can turn left or right onto William, so “left only” keeps the left and removes the right. That makes sense. On Rue William, from either side, a car can only go straight on, since Chatham is one-way towards William. There “left only” would remove the only move and trap every car. So the signs belong to Chatham.
The rule is this: a turn sign belongs to a street only when it keeps at least one move the street has and removes at least one. If several streets pass, two things decide. First, panels on one post usually face the same drivers, so if the post also carries a stop sign and the turn sign means something on that street, it goes there. Then position: a sign before the junction, on the right, is preferred, and a sign past the junction is used only when nothing before it fits.
Two panels on one post that contradict each other, like “straight only” above “left or right only”, cannot face the same drivers. They stand back to back, so the second one looks for another street. If there is none, it gets no street and a place on the list to check. Only a photo can tell which way each one faces.
A turn sign at an exit is ignored, because the streets it points to lie outside the network. If several turn signs on one street together leave no move at all, S3 sets them aside and keeps every move open. After the photos, no street is in that state.
My first version placed turn signs by position alone, like stop signs, and left many streets with no way out. One of the stress tests repeats that version so the difference stays visible.
To name a turn, S3 compares the direction a car is heading as it arrives with the direction of the street it leaves along. Less than 30° either way counts as straight on. Anything sharper is a left or a right. From Chatham onto William the heading turns 89° to the left. S3 never makes a U-turn.

title: How S3 is built
text:
Decisions from photos
A few signs could not be placed from the desk. For those I looked at Mapillary’s photos and wrote down what I saw (the photo checks). S3 reads those decisions before its own matching, so a photo outranks a guess. The city’s file is never edited, so removing a decision brings back S3’s own matching.

title: How S3 is built
text:
No-entry signs
A no-entry sign stands at the mouth of a street a car may not enter. S1 already knows the one-way streets from the city, so S3 uses these signs only to check S1. A sign agrees when a street near it is one-way towards the junction, or closed to cars. If only a path I added in S1 explains it, it goes on the list to check, because my own decision cannot confirm itself.

title: How S3 is built
text:
Traffic lights
The city’s light file gives each light a point and the names of the streets it stands between. S3 gives each light to the closest junction within 25 m. A light between 25 and 100 m from every junction goes on the list to check, because it may point to a junction S1 is missing.
The street names give a second check: “Montagne / Wellington” should stand where Rue de la Montagne meets Rue Wellington. The file says nothing about timing, so that belongs to S7, as an assumption.

title: How S3 is built
text:
Speed limits
The city’s speed file uses the same street ids as S1, so most segments simply take the limit written on their own line.
Two things need care. Seven segments have a limit of 0 in the file, and all seven are closed to cars, so S3 reads 0 as “no limit given” and leaves the limit empty. And three Wellington pieces were redrawn after the speed file was made, so they have new ids. For those, S3 looks for lines of the same street name lying along the segment, within 5 m. If they cover nearly all of it and agree on one speed, S3 takes that speed.
The 5 m is the smallest distance that covers the two short pieces where Wellington splits. I chose it by looking at those three segments, and a stress test shows what other distances would give.

title: S3 Rules
text:
S3 gives the S1 streets their traffic rules. Picture a driver arriving at a junction. S3 answers four questions for them: must I stop here, are there traffic lights, where may I go next, and how fast may I drive. It reads three of the city’s files to find out, and every rule points back to the sign or city record it came from.
Lights and speed limits are the easy part, because the city lists them directly. Stops and turns are hard. The city’s sign file says where each sign stands and what it says. It never says which street a sign faces, and a sign at a corner often stands close to two or three streets at once. S3 has to work that out, and how S3 is built explains how.
The tests ask whether the result holds up, and the photo checks settle the few places I could not decide from the desk.

title: S3 Rules
text:
One junction, step by step
Junction J027 is where Rue Chatham ends at Rue William, in the west of Griffintown.



Rue Chatham is one-way towards William and must stop. Its two turn signs allow only the left. Click to enlarge.



Three street ends touch J027: Rue Chatham, and Rue William on each side of it. A car can arrive along all of them, so S3 makes three approaches. An approach is simply one way of arriving at a junction: one street, driven towards the corner.
The sign file has a stop sign on a post near the corner. Measured from Rue Chatham, it stands 10 m before the junction and 5 m to the right. That is where a stop sign for Chatham would stand, and it fits no other street. So Rue Chatham must stop.
Two more posts carry “left turn only” signs. Both stand on the right of Rue Chatham, 4 to 8 m before the junction.
From Chatham a car can leave along William to the left or to the right. S3 names each move by how much the car’s heading changes: about 90° to the left is a left.
The signs allow only the left. So the left onto William is allowed, and the right onto William is forbidden, with the reason written beside it.
One end of Rue William has its own stop sign and the other has none. So at J027 some streets stop, and there are no lights.

title: S3 Rules
text:
Places still to check
The 21 places still to check fall into five groups. Seven are Autoroute 10 and its ramps, which the city’s speed file does not cover. Six are signs I could not give to any street. Three are photo decisions the photos could not settle (still open). Three are lights just beyond the edge, such as the one at Queen and Wellington. Two are recent no-entry posts at the park connectors, newer than every photo.
Signs at exits that face streets beyond the network are not on the list: they are not mine to check.

title: S3 Rules
text:
What S3 does not know
The city’s file says where the lights are and nothing about their timing. Movement counts and light timing estimates it where the city counted traffic. Elsewhere the cycle will be a procedural assumption in S7.
Some turn rules hold only at certain hours. S3 keeps them on at all hours until S5 Rhythm gives the simulation a clock.
At exits, streets beyond the network meet the junction, and S3 cannot see them. So a junction there may look like an all-way stop when a street beyond does not stop. The junction’s note says so.

The city’s files are open under CC BY 4.0 and OpenStreetMap under ODbL.
I looked at two more and set them aside. The Concordia NGCI building file has no licence, so I cannot publish anything made from it. It also records each condo tower as a single property: 2199 rue Ann, 76 m tall, appears as one dwelling. The other was Québec City’s building file, which does not cover Montréal.
I also opened the city’s 3D model of 2020 (Bâtiments 3D 2020, CityGML). It measures every roof, which would replace the storey counts with heights in metres. But the 2020 model covers only Ville-Marie, Outremont and Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, and Griffintown sits in Le Sud-Ouest. Of its tiles, four reach the edge of the study area, and they hold three small structures by Rue Notre-Dame (certain). For Le Sud-Ouest the city published the 2016 model, which is older than most of the towers here. I have not used it yet.

title: How S4 is built
text:
The problem
Every source here is a list of points or rows. Only OpenStreetMap draws buildings. So before anything else, S4 has to give each row a building.

title: How S4 is built
text:
Step 1: the outlines
A building belongs to the study area when the centre of its outline falls inside the boundary.
Sometimes OpenStreetMap draws a tower as a second outline on top of its podium. Griffix on Rue Wellington is one: a 2-storey base, and a 21-storey tower drawn over it. When the centre of one outline lies inside a larger one, S4 treats the smaller as a part of the larger, not as a building of its own.

title: How S4 is built
section: Step 2: the tax roll at its address
text:
Step 2: the tax roll at its address
The roll gives each property a street name and a number. The city’s address points give a position for a range of numbers on a named street, so S4 matches the two. Many roll rows found no match, because I downloaded the roll for whole streets across the island and the address points only around Griffintown.
I used to think none of the missed rows stood in the study area. The lot outlines showed otherwise: 64 rows have their land in the study area and no address point there. They count now, through their lot.

title: How S4 is built
section: Step 3: every row finds its building
text:
Step 3: every row finds its building
The city publishes the roll a second time with the outline of each property’s lot, the piece of land it is taxed on. Every condo unit in a building repeats the lot it shares with its neighbours. A lot is firmer ground than an address point, which is a single dot the city places near a door or a curb.
So S4 reads the lot first. The buildings on a lot are those whose centre the lot holds. When none does, a building that covers at least 30% of the lot counts.

When the lot holds one building, the row goes there.
When it holds several, the address point says which. If the point stands in none of them, the nearest within 15 m takes it. Beyond that the row stays unplaced, with the reason.
When the lot holds no building, the address point works alone: inside an outline, or the nearest one within 15 m.

The lot and the address point sometimes disagree. When the lot holds one building, I let the lot decide. When it holds several and the point stands in a building off the lot, I let the point decide, since the lot cannot choose. Both cases go on my list of checkpoints, ten of them so far.
Griffix is why this step changed. Its 197 flats, at 1045 rue Wellington, have their address point inside MaryRobert next door, so S4 used to count them there. Their lot holds Griffix and nothing else. They now live in Griffix, and MaryRobert drops from 678 dwellings to 491.
Why 15 m? With no reach at all, 1,322 rows would be left out. At 15 m, 468 are, and 415 of those share one address point that stands 130 m from the two towers on their lot (checkpoint B01). Doubling the reach to 30 m places two more. The further the reach, the more a point risks joining the wrong building.

title: How S4 is built
text:
Step 4: the use
The roll gives every property a land-use code whose first digit names a broad family, such as residential or commerce. The commonest family among a building’s properties becomes its use, leaving out condo parking spaces and storage units. A tie goes to the larger floor area, and a missing area is never read as zero. When the roll cannot decide, the OpenStreetMap tag speaks next. A plain “building” tag names no use, so the use stays empty, with the reason.
Every tie goes on my list to check by hand, because it often means two buildings share one outline. Ardent Mills is an example: the roll places a 74-dwelling social housing property and the flour mill inside the same outline.

title: How S4 is built
text:
Step 5: size
A building is as tall as its tallest known part. S4 compares the storeys the roll gives, the storeys on the OpenStreetMap outline, and the storeys of every OpenStreetMap part inside it, and keeps the largest, noting where it came from. Condo units are left out of this, since the roll gives each unit only its own floor.
I added the parts after an audit. Before, MaryRobert’s 678 dwellings stood in a building of 2 storeys, because the outline carried only its podium. Now it reads 22, from its tower. Where no part gives a better number and the dwellings cannot fit, S4 puts the building on my list to check.
Dwellings are the sum of the roll’s dwellings over the building’s properties.

title: How S4 is built
text:
Step 6: ground floor and places
The premises are the 2025 survey’s spaces inside the building, vacant ones included. The places are anywhere a person might go. Some come from OpenStreetMap, and the others are the city’s public places and the survey’s occupied shops. Benches and bike racks are left out.
Sometimes the survey and OpenStreetMap list the same shop. When the two carry exactly the same name in the same building, S4 links them as one place. A looser match, like Orangetheory Fitness against Orangetheory Theory, is left alone: it would be a guess.

title: How S4 is built
text:
Step 7: the access link
For each building, S4 finds the nearest S1 street people can walk on, within 80 m. This stands in for the door. It is the weakest value in S4, and every building’s record says so.

title: S4 tests
text:
Each check asks one plain question of the finished buildings.







Question
Answer




Does every outline in the study area appear exactly once, as a building or as a part of the building around it?
Yes: 296 buildings, and one tower drawn over its podium


Does every missing value stay empty with a reason, and every value name its source?
Yes


Can every count be rebuilt from the source files?
Yes


Is every property and shop in the area either in one building or listed as unplaced, never both and never twice?
Yes


Does each use follow the rule for its source, ties included?
Yes


Is every building linked to a walkable street within 80 m, or does it say why not?
Yes. Six links are longer than 30 m, and Hangar 1825 has none.


Is every place in or next to its building, and does every shop listed twice point to its twin?
Yes, with 52 such pairs


Is any building lower than its tallest known part?
No. Nine take their storeys from a tower part


Does every property sit on its lot: in the building its lot holds, or where its address point stands, with a checkpoint whenever the two disagree?
Yes



One more check only reports how much the sources cover. A gap there is a fact about the sources, and never a failure. The Lab shows the latest results.
Two of these checks changed the work. The fourth one failed on its first run: it found 89 properties counted twice. The cause was my download. The tax roll came in pages, and some pages overlapped. S4 now keeps one row per property.
The use check changed after the first run too. Looking at the map of uses, I saw Ardent Mills, the flour mill, painted residential. The roll puts two properties in its outline, one residential and one industrial, and my first rule broke the tie by the order of a list. That was a choice I never made on purpose. Now a tie goes to the larger floor area, and a missing floor area settles nothing. After that the OpenStreetMap tag speaks, and every tie goes on my list to check by hand.






TipTesting the tests



A test that always passes proves nothing. So I broke the finished buildings file four ways and ran the checks again. I removed the reason from an unknown use, added one dwelling to a building, changed one use that came from the roll, and wrote 0 into an empty dwelling count. The checks caught all four. Then I put the file back.


The last check came from an audit. I set MaryRobert back to 2 storeys in the file, and the check named it at once: a part of it has 22.
The audit found one more problem, in the arithmetic. S4 found the centre of each outline from map coordinates in the millions of metres, and multiplying such large numbers lost the small digits. Most centres were less than a metre off, but some were off by tens of metres. That had made four small outlines look as if they stood inside their neighbours. S4 now measures each outline from its own first corner, and the false overlaps are gone.

title: S4 tests
text:
Stress tests
These ask how much the result depends on my choices.
Running S4 twice on the same input gives the same output, line for line.
The 15 m reach, within which a stray point joins the nearest building, matters a lot at first and then very little. With no reach at all, 1,322 rows would be left out. At 15 m, 468 are, 415 of them at the one address point of checkpoint B01. Doubling the reach to 30 m places two more, without moving any property to a different building.
The last test shakes every address point by 2 m, then by 5 m, as if the city had placed them a little off. At 2 m, 244 properties change building; at 5 m, 278 do. The total of dwellings stays at 11,954.
The earlier figure at 5 m was 625, and it was partly an accident of the test. Each point’s random move depended on the order in which the points were read, so adding the lots reshuffled every move. Each address point now gets its own fixed move, whatever the order. With that fix, the run without lots gives 291 at 5 m, so the lots barely change this number (certain). Most properties sit on lots that hold several buildings, where the address point still decides.
That result is the warning. All the units at one address point move together, as one point. Where two buildings share a wall, an address point a little off lands in the neighbour, and a condo tower’s hundreds of units go with it. So a single building’s count can be wrong while the block’s total is right. S5 and S6 should read dwellings by block, or with that in mind.

title: S4 tests
text:
The Lab check
The Lab keeps its own copy of the S4 results, so I added a check that the two match exactly, down to every outline point, and that an empty value stays empty. I broke the Lab’s copy four ways: I turned an unknown dwelling count into 0, changed one use, moved one outline point by 1 m, and dropped one place. The check caught all four.

title: Why I use it
text: A simulation can use space syntax as a steering wheel, where the agents read the values and prefer high-scoring streets. That is circular: the answer goes in, so the same answer comes out. I use it as a measuring stick. My agents never read the values, and I compare their movement with the values afterwards, which makes the comparison a real test.

title: Why I use it
text:
The circle
Choice is already a route model: it counts the route with the least turning between every pair of segments (Turner 2007, p. 544). If my walkers also took those routes, spread evenly over all pairs, they would match choice by construction, and the match would prove nothing. So the walkers in S6 pick routes for their own reasons, such as where they are going and the time of day. Space syntax enters Situ only at the end, in S8 Observer.

Where the walkers and choice agree, the layout alone may explain the movement. Where they disagree, something else is at work, such as a building or a rule.


The city’s counts check the model against reality, and they are thin: seven S1 junctions, one to three days each, between February 2024 and May 2026 (Movement counts). That is enough to raise a warning and too little to prove anything.


In the game I can watch whether players drift toward integrated streets. This links to my research question on wayfinding.

title: Why I use it
text:
Why this method
It runs on the city’s open street file in QGIS, and the same file with the same settings gives the same values. Forty years of studies use it, so I can set Griffintown beside other cities. It was built to study how layout and social life relate, which is the subject of my research. Its blind spots are well documented, and each one maps onto another Situ system.

title: Why I use it
section: What this means for my data
text:
What this means for my data
Values belong to the network they were calculated on. A missing path makes its neighbours look less connected than they are, so I added the city’s off-street paths before the analysis (The walking network).
The edge of the map also distorts. Streets near it look peripheral only because the map stops there (Ratti 2004, p. 496; van Nes & Yamu 2021, p. 51). So the analysis covers the whole island, and I cut Griffintown out of the results afterwards.
